utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom and outside, but it's only for a short moment that we are in open session. The next witness will be heard in closed session. Are there any matters to raise by the parties? If that is not the case, we should go into closed session. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May there be peace in this house for all those present and may God's will be done into these proceedings and may the outcome be as God wishes and not as I wish. Mr. President, I have been informed by my legal assistant about the following witness. The Defence intended to submit a response to the Prosecution's motion about increasing the protective measures for the witness who now has a designation 074. The OTP, in addition to a distorted image and voice, also wanted a closed session testimony, but we would oppose to this motion. The decision was made without allowing the Defence to respond in any way whatsoever, and there was no dead-line for submitting a response to the Prosecution's motion. The Defence has not been allowed to state its position, which in the Defence's view opposes the right of the accused to a fair trial and especially his right to respond properly to any request by the Prosecution. I also wish to point out that in the situation where we do not have much time, abilities ought to be provided both -- to both parties to submit their requests, and I believe that proceeding in this way would not prevent the accused from defending. We shall respect the decision of the Trial Chamber because I cannot change it, but we do not believe that the Prosecution should question any of the witnesses in closed session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, Mr. McCloskey, do you want to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. We have nothing to add to the Appellate Chamber's decision. Closed session is something that the Prosecution does not favour, but when the circumstances warrant it, we will apply to the appropriate Chamber for those measures, should the circumstances warrant it. This is one of those extraordinary or exceptional circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you will realise that not the -- this Trial Chamber has rendered this decision but the Appeals Chamber who is seised of the relevant first proceedings. We are bound by that. We have no discretion to decide in a different way than the Appeals Chamber. I think we should proceed. It is not up to the Chamber to decide anything on that matter. We are now going into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I respect the decision of the Appeals Chamber, but I shall not examine the witness in closed session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are again in open session. We have to discuss a procedural matter. And first of all, Mr. Tolimir, the Chamber would like to know your position, how you want to deal with the Appeals Chamber decision on protective measures. Are you intending to challenge this decision of the Appeals Chamber in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have told you that I respect any decision of the Appeals Chamber. I respect the decisions of all Trial Chambers, including the Appeals Chamber. I have not been allowed to follow the procedure, and I shall not examine the witness in closed session. I will not even complain. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This Chamber is not in a position to discuss the proceeding before the Appeals Chamber. We are bound by the decision of the Appeals Chamber. We just want to know that you -- if you want to challenge this decision by any means. I take it now that you are not going to challenge the decision of the Appeals Chamber; did I understand you correctly? Thank you. You are nodding. In this case, there will be no different decision --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it is necessary for the transcript, let me say that I will not challenge it. I respect the decisions of the Appeals Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Even if we would postpone the examination of this witness, we will not find ourselves in a different situation. The Appeals Chamber has rule on the application of the OTP and therefore if we hear the witness today, tomorrow, next week, or after the summer recess, there's no different situation. This witness has to be heard in closed session. Then we could proceed and go into closed session. Mr. Thayer first.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I am a little unclear about what General Tolimir's position is going to be with respect to actually examining this witness. We've heard him say that he respects the Appeals Chamber's decision, but he will not, he says, examine this witness in closed session. It's unclear to me, at least, what that means. If it means that for some reason General Tolimir is going to be standing down and somehow going on strike and refusing to exercise his right of cross-examination because of the Appeals Chamber decision, because he disagrees with it, number one, that's inconsistent with the position he's taken; number two, we need to make that clear on the record that that is in fact what's happening. And if that's in fact what's happening, then that raises a larger issue for the future of this trial, where we may have witnesses for whom closed session measures will be requested. That's -- if it does happen, that's going to be a very small number of witnesses, I can assure Your Honours, but I think it is very problematic to have the accused essentially say, Well, if that's the way the Appeals Chamber is going to rule, then I'm going to take my marbles and go home and not play. And if he wants to do that, that's his right as an accused. However, we need to have that on the record. He needs to be made clear that that is what he's doing, that he's doing that knowingly and willfully. However, that also, in itself, I think, potentially sets a dangerous precedent for the conduct of the trial if he continues to take such positions where if he disagrees with something he decides that he is not going to participate any more. I think we all share the desire to ensure that as -- particularly as a self-represented accused, his fair rights are being preserved. And I just want some clarity for the record about what he intends to do and what his position is for this witness and for the sake of future witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, do you want to respond?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I do not wish to play marbles here. Let me repeat again my last sentence, which was that the Defence was not allowed to express its view on this very significant matter. And in the Defence's view, this opposes the basic rights of the accused to a fair and expeditious trial, especially the accused's right to have the opportunity to follow the procedure as envisaged by the rules and respond to the request of the OTP. That was all I had to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The Chamber's indulgence. I just want to make the Prosecution's position as clear as possible on this. The Prosecution has no objection were General Tolimir to decide to engage in some appellate review of its decision. We've got no problem with that. We've got no problem with him exercising any of his rights to which is he is entitled under the statute and the practice of this Tribunal. However, as you've indicated, Mr. President, whatever he decides to do in the Appellate Chamber or anywhere else has no bearing whatsoever as far as we can see upon the ability for this Trial Chamber to proceed with this witness today. The only practical consequence of any future proceedings would be basically to unseal closed testimony. It does not effect General Tolimir's ability to cross-examine this witness, prepare for this witness, or in any other way represent himself with respect to this witness's testimony. I just wanted to make that clear, number one. Number 2, we've heard now a couple of times the representation by General Tolimir that he was not allowed to somehow participate in this -- in this litigation with respect to our application for closed session. That is simply incorrect. He was properly placed on notice of this urgent motion. The Popovic team managed to file a response before the Appeals Chamber. We understand that everybody is working under time constraints, but to suggest that he was denied some opportunity to participate or to have his position articulated is simple incorrect. He just didn't move fast enough under the obvious urgency of the motion that was filed, and the Appellate Chamber issued its ruling. We had no indication that there was going to be any objection by the Defence to this. And, again, if he wants a second bite at the apple, as it were, before the Appeals Chamber, no problem. But that should not slow us down in any way. And, again, General Tolimir has not clarified what he plans to do when this witness comes in here and we get through the 92 procedure. Is he going to proceed with the cross-examination or not? And if this accused cannot abide by some of the most fundamental precepts of this institution to -- he gives lip service to respecting any and all decisions by Chambers, but if he cannot abide by those simple rules and he is going to sit down and go home if he doesn't get his way, then at some point we may need to reconsider whether his self-representation status is appropriate, because it risks just stopping these proceedings if he persists. Now, again, this could be just a one-shot problem that we're looking at, but he's had a couple of opportunities to do so and he has not articulated what he plans to do. That causes me great concern. If he can't tell the Trial Chamber, I'm going to cross-examine this witness, I'm going to abide by the decision of the Appeals Chamber and go ahead and exercise my right of cross-examination; if there's an alternative that he wants to pursue, he needs to articulate that. We need to know. And he refuses to do that, again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just expressed my view a little while ago. I told you what I think about the procedure according to which this decision was made. Mr. Thayer is trying to convince me that I should change my decision. He says the Appeals Chamber decided that Mr. Tolimir should cross-examine. The Appeals Chamber decided that the testimony should be in closed session and not that Tolimir has to question the witness. So please let us not discuss whether I respect something or not. The Appeals Chamber decided that this would be in closed session. I told you what I think about the procedure. The second thing, it is true that I did not receive it in time because it still has not been translated. If it's just one page, then I could have received both the English original and the B/C/S translation. As the accused, I have not been informed about this because I did not receive the translation. So please take into account what I said and let us not waste time. I apologise, I have told my assistant that I would submit a request in accordance with the procedure, and I announced this to the OTP three days ago. And the OTP knew that I would submit a response to such procedure. Thank you. That I would appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please explain the last sentence; I didn't understand that perfectly because ... did you indicate to the Prosecution that you will -- sorry, I didn't finish yet. You had a discussion with your legal advisor. I just want to know, Did you indicate to the Prosecution that you will raise this problem before this Chamber or if you would intend to appeal in any way to the Appeals Chamber? What did you indicate to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Three days ago, I announced to the Prosecution that the Defence would submit a response to the Prosecution's motion that this witness be questioned in closed session. However, we were not allowed to do that. The Appeals Chamber did not respect the rules, and ruled as it did. I do not know if the OTP knew this or not, if it asked for an urgent decision. I'm just telling you what my legal assistant and myself did in consultation. And this is all I wanted to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, another question, Mr. Tolimir: Did you give any indication to the Appeals Chamber that you are intending to respond to the Prosecution motions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If I responded to the Appeals Chamber, first I would have had to have the document translated. I could not have used it as a reference because I did not receive the Prosecution's motion. It has not been translated to this day. I cannot write anything without a proper reference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the Chamber would like to make the situation very clear. There is, I think, at least in the transcript, a contradiction. First you said you will respect the Appeals Chamber's decision and will not challenge it; and then - and that is on page 9, line 6 - you said that, I would appeal. Could you tell, please, the OTP and the Chamber what is your intention? Will you in any way challenge the decision of the Appeals Chamber or not? This is the key question. We need to know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think that I was quite clear. In my first intervention, I said that I will respect the decision of the Appeals Chamber and I do not intend to challenge it. And that's what I answered when you asked a follow-up question when the session continued. Now, I had indicated that I would appeal the decision before the Appeals Chamber rendered its decision, not that I would appeal. That I would respond to the Prosecution motion. So I did not say that I would appeal. I said that I would respond to the Prosecution motion, but that was before the Appeals Chamber ruled. Now that the decision is here, I don't intend to appeal or to challenge it, but I intend to exercise my right not to examine this witness in closed session because the procedure has been violated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The debate shows that we are faced -- facing a very difficult problem and therefore we have to continue to put some questions. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I have a question for General Tolimir. Would you like to have an opportunity to be heard in the matter that was before the Appeals Chamber in any way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, I would like to ask the Honourable Judge to repeat her question because it appears to have been misinterpreted into the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay. You have indicated in your submissions that you have some concerns with the fact that you were not allowed to express your view on this very significant matter, which is correct. Would you, therefore, like to be given the opportunity to be heard and express your views on this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have expressed my view orally here in the courtroom in my two interventions, and I do not intend to challenge the decision of the Appeals Chamber. And I'm not happy that the Appeals Chamber ruled without first hearing the Defence on the issue of the procedure regarding this Prosecution motion, because we have indicated -- we had indicated to the Prosecution we would respond to this motion, but we had not been given an opportunity. And we had not even received the motion, in fact. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Therefore, I understand from your response and really for the avoidance of doubt, that you have no intention to ask for review or appeal against the Appeals Chamber decision, but that merely you are just protesting the way the decision was reached without hearing you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am a Christian, and I accept any decision whether it's detrimental or not detrimental to my case. And I do not want to challenge any decision, although I suffer the consequences of each and every one. So please bear that in mind when we talk about that. I said that I would not challenge the Appeals Chamber decision. That's how they ruled. I will just bear the consequences. And that's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I think the Chamber would like to put it on record that as proposed by the Prosecution that you do have the right to be heard and in this case you could go to the Appeals Chamber to ask for review or appeal against it. And I take your answer to mean you are waiving that right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I did not say that I waive my right. I said that, as a Christian, I accept all decisions of the appropriate bodies of this Tribunal, including the Appeals Chamber. And if they do not respect my rights, I will bear the consequences of that fact. And that's all I said. Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We see the situation the accused finds himself in after the decision of the Appeals Chamber. This Chamber was not seised of that, has no stand in making this decision, and we don't comment the Appeals Chamber decision, so that there's no room for in the alternative way. We would like to proceed and move into closed session now, and the witness should be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are in open session again, and let's continue with the next witness. He should be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Welcome to the Tribunal. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey has some questions for you, I suppose. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, and everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Celanovic.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you state your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Zlatan Celanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you had a chance in the last day or so to review your testimony from the Popovic trial that you did back in 2007?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you were asked those same questions again, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was the information you provided in that testimony true and correct to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I would offer in what has been numbered P637, the transcript of that former testimony. And if I could read the witness summary, and then I would offer in the other items with a brief explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The transcript of the Popovic trial will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please indicate the number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Celanovic, as you know, there's a little summary I'll read. And I will try to get it right, as you recall it. But if there's any changes you would like to make, let us know. But this is meant to be a summary of your last testimony. Okay?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Zlatan Celanovic was born on 18 February 1955 in Bratunac. He is a lawyer by profession and practices law in Bratunac. He served in the VRS Bratunac Brigade during the war in Bosnia. In July 1995, he was working in the moral, legal, and religious branch of the Bratunac Brigade. His immediate superior was Major Ratko Jevtic, assistant commander for moral, legal, and religious affairs of the Bratunac Brigade. His commander was Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic, commander of the Bratunac Brigade. In July 1995, Celanovic was the Bratunac Brigade desk officer for this branch. At times, Mr. Celanovic worked with Captain Momir Nikolic, the Bratunac Brigade chief of security and intelligence. Mr. Celanovic also worked with the military police and dealt with breaches of military discipline committed by soldiers. His responsibility was to take statements from persons brought to him by the military police and to deliver those statements to the commander who would make a decision as to whether charges would be brought. He also had intelligence and counter-intelligence responsibilities. On the evening of 12 July or the morning of 13 July 1995 - Mr. Celanovic could not be sure which time was correct - he met with Ljubisa Beara in front of the military police building near the Bratunac Brigade headquarters. He knew Beara from previous visits Beara had made to the brigade in 1993 and 1994 and testified that Beara was either a colonel or a lieutenant-colonel, he wasn't sure. At that time, Beara asked Celanovic if he had any information about Muslims who had committed crimes against the Serbian people. Mr. Celanovic responded that there was a book entitled "Chronicle of Our Cemetery" that had the names of Muslims in it. Beara asked him to identify Muslims if in the course of the day they were brought to the MP building, or otherwise taken into military police custody, and to check and determine if their names appeared in this book. Beara told Celanovic that if he identified someone from the book, he was to inform the security organ so that action may be taken and the case forwarded to the competent military prosecutor. On the morning of 13 July, Momir Nikolic brought Muslim prisoner Resid Sinanovic, a Bosnian Muslim lawyer from the -- and the former chief of public security station or police station in Bratunac. Nikolic brought him to the military police building and asked Mr. Celanovic to investigate allegations of war crimes committed by Sinanovic. Soon after Sinanovic's arrival there, five or six other Bosnian Muslim prisoners were delivered to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters by soldiers that Mr. Celanovic described as "Special Forces." The names of the Bosnian Muslim men were Nazif Avdic, Munib Dedic, Aziz Husic, Mujo Husic, and Hasib Ibisevic. These five men were taken first, and then one and a half hours later Sinanovic was taken there, according to the witness who clarified that recently. And these men are named in paragraphs 21.1 of the third amended indictment, Your Honours. Mr. Celanovic questioned all six Bosnian Muslim men and took notes of the interrogation. Mr. Celanovic identified his interview notes in court proceedings during Popovic trial and affirmed that they reflect the men he interviewed. And, for the record, the exhibit numbers of his notes are P638 through 641. And I'll mention them a bit later. After the interrogations, Sinanovic and the other Muslim prisoners were taken to the Vuk Karadzic School in Bratunac, a short distance away. During the day on 13 July, Mr. Celanovic observed trucks and buses in Bratunac full of Muslim men who had been taken prisoner. The evening of 13 July, Mr. Celanovic met Ljubisa Beara for the second time at the front of the military police building near the Bratunac Brigade command. Mr. Celanovic testified -- excuse me, Mr. Celanovic reported to Beara that he had seen Muslims in buses and trucks in Bratunac that day. Then, at about dusk, Mr. Celanovic and Mr. Beara walked to the Bratunac stadium and elementary school area where they observed trucks and buses full of Muslim men. Soldiers were securing these vehicles and the people in them. Mr. Celanovic asked Mr. Beara why these people were not being transported immediately. Beara responded that there were not enough vehicles to transport them and that a re-organisation of the transport was being carried out and that their women and children would go to Kladanj the next morning. Shortly thereafter, Mr. Celanovic and Colonel Beara returned to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters. And that is the end of my summary. And, Mr. President, I would offer those notes of the interviews of those Muslim men that were referred to in the testimony and as were just referred to in the summary, and those would be number 638 for Mr. Husic; 639 for Mr. Sinanovic; 640 for Abdic, Dedic, Husic, and a person named Begzadic; 641, notes of Ibisevic; in addition, 642, which was a letter which attached a medical record that is related to Mr. Sinanovic; and 643, which is an aerial image of Bratunac that was described and marked by the witness. Also, going to a different grouping of materials, I would offer P644, which -- only pages 4 and 5, because this was a large statement of facts from Momir Nikolic and pages 4 and 5 were read out to Mr. Nikolic [sic] in cross-examination by the Defence, and I'm not offering the entire statement but for 4 and 5 so you can see how that worked. Sorry, they were read out to Mr. Celanovic during his cross, not to Mr. Nikolic. And I've spoken with Mr. Gajic on that, and he agreed that it was appropriate to have those two pages, as opposed to the entire statement. I would also offer P645 which was another document that was used in cross by the Defence, but I think it makes more sense to have the entire document for that. Also, lastly, P646 which was a statement that Mr. Celanovic gave to the Bratunac police in 2003, but I'm only offering pages 3 and 4 because those were the parts that were shown to him by the Defence during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: All these documents with the given P numbers will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could put P643 up on the e-court. That is this aerial image.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Celanovic, I don't want to completely redo this. There's a pretty clear record of this. But do you recall what basically were you -- when you were - and this image will come up on this, and we'll explain it in a little more detail, but -- there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could blow that up more, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this has been marked before. It's very difficult to see. So I think we need to blow it up a bit more. And it's that big building up in the left-hand corner. If we could blow that up, you'll -- you'll -- one more time, I think. You'll be able to see some of these markings a bit better. That's good. If we could centre that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, first of all, Mr. Celanovic, what was -- what is this aerial image of? What town are we looking at here?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is -- do you recognise these green marks as markings that you made in the last trial?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So let's explain these briefly for this Trial Chamber. First of all, we see this very large rectangular angular thing that has a little green rectangle at the end of it. Can you tell us what this big building is, this big rectangular white building that has the green markings on one end?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: That is the building in which the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade was accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was it before the war, that huge building?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, it was an administrative buildings. There were offices there, and these were the offices of the Kaolin factory. They had their business premises there. The management and the administrative staff were accommodated there on the top floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Could you -- and I think we should mark this one. Could you put a 1 by the rectangle that indicates where the offices were. I think, if you remember how to do that, I think it's basically the same as it was when you testified, but he'll help you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Court Officer will assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is, number 1. The right side of the building -- I mean the floor. And also the ground floor in the right half of the building was the office of the brigade commander. At the ground floor was the duty officer's room, and on the right-hand side on the ground floor was the mess for the members of the Bratunac Brigade. Whereas on the left side, on the floor - let me mark it this way - were the officers' rooms for the personnel department as well as the logistics officers' rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That little notch you made for the logistics officers' rooms, can just put a 2 by that so that anyone looking at the record will see what that is.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it visible?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think so, yes. So to be clear, what we are looking at within that rectangle is a two-story building attached to the Kaolin factory that is -- was for administrative offices. And now, during the war, it was military offices; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this other huge building that it's attached to, that -- you've described that as the Kaolin factory. What did they make there, before the war?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Ceramic tiles were being produced there before the war in the big facility or should I say a series of facilities behind. Should I mark that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, that's okay. I just wanted -- wanted us to know, get a feel for what that huge building was about. More importantly, we see, going back to where the brigade offices were, that you have marked it's almost a square in front. Can you put a 3 by that square and tell us what that -- what building or what you were noting in that area?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: That was the reception desk room. That was where the person who was working at the gate was located. And that was, at the same time, the gate to the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where is the military police building that you talk about in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: In the building marked with number 2. It is this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you've marked number 2 as where the logistics officers were, so let's mark the number 4, the one that you just marked, which you have now said was the military police building.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we can also see from this diagram that the green line goes from the area of the front of the gate, follows the road for a while. Can you briefly tell us what that was supposed to depict, that green line and -- as it disappears off our page, and we'll get into that in a little more detail.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: That is the access road leading to the Kaolin factory. Or, in this case, the headquarters of the brigade and also the military police leading from Gavrila Principa Street all the way to the entrance gate, that is, the gate to the factory or the gate leading to the headquarters of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember being asked to draw the route that you and Colonel Beara took when you left that evening on the 13th and walked into the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that depicted by the green line as it's going along the streets?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we put this blow-up into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received with markings of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P652.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could pan out with the original shot so we can get an idea of where they walked to. Hoping not to lose these markings, of course. Okay. We can see the Kaolin factory, but we need to blow it up a bit more if we're going to get an idea of his former green line and the route they took. All right. Yeah, if you can move it up a little more because we can ... just a little bit more, please. One more smidge. Just a couple more centimetres. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So I think everyone can see that -- that green line. And as you walk out from the gate, you took a right on that main street. What was the main street that you took a right on that we can see the green line going down?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: That is Gavrila Principa Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I don't want to go through your testimony; I think it's clear. But can you point out to the Court, just put a big F where the football stadium is.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. As I'm left-handed, I have to try to do it with my right hand because it's not really visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can see that big field where you've put that F. And, now, can you put a big X by the Vuk Kar -- what was known then, as you've testified, as the Vuk Karadzic School and surrounding buildings. Just put a big X on the top of the Vuk Karadzic School, if you can spot it.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And one more location that the Trial Chamber's heard a lot about, can you put a big circle around the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just a second so I can find my bearings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this photo into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, we're not --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P644 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're not precisely sure of the date of this aerial photo, but it is sometime in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the number has to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. The correct number is P653.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, do you have cross-examination for the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I do have questions. I wish to greet the witness. I hope that the witness would feel pleasant here, God bless you, and I hope that the proceedings would finish in accordance with God's will and not in accordance with my own will. So please tell us the truth, because you are a lawyer by profession. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we both speak the same language, please pause a little while, once I finish my question and say thank you, until you can see that the transcript in English has finished with my last words. I will also try to wait for your answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: First of all, let us explore this. I have, in front of me, a statement, 1D1 -- 212.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to see it on the screen. 1D564, in fact. I would like to -- P646.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is 1D00219.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we can see the statement here. Is this the statement that you gave, record, is this your signature on the front page? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, based on the signature, I would say that it is, but it's a little bit illegible, so if you could maybe zoom in a little bit. Now it's fine. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please repeat your question, it was not --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, yes, I apologise. I failed to switch on the microphone. Let us look at page 2 so that the witness can confirm whether this is indeed his signature. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, I asked you whether this was your signature.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like us to look at page 3 of this statement of yours. Thank you. Well, we can see the first paragraph on page 3. I will recount what you say here. You say in line 3 that you were the desk officer for moral, religious, and legal affairs - that's at page 2 in the English version - and that you were in charge of administrative duties, and that you were on stand-by for those administrative tasks; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell us for the record whether you took part in combat at all, or, rather, whether you only performed those administrative tasks that you told us about? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did take part in the fighting when there were attacks on the Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. I wanted to ask you if you took part in the fighting in July 1995; that's the time-period that your statement refers to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like you to look at paragraph 6 of your statement in the Serbian language. Or, rather, page 4, I'm sorry. So that would be page 4 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which paragraph on page 4? Is it paragraph 6?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, yes, paragraph 6. Line 6 in the English version, that's page 3, the last, sixth, line at the very end of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say that it was your assessment that the town was not secure since all the troops were out on the ground, and you say this was a realistic fact and knowing that the security officer, that was Colonel Beara, presented his views, but Colonel Beara, however, said, It's all right, both we and they will make it through the night, and tomorrow they are going to Kladanj for sure. Thank you. Did I quote you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes. Now, it's been scrolled down so now you can read it, but you've already answered my question. Now I have another question, a follow-up question: Why did you think that Sarajevo was not safe at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Bratunac was not safe at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What was the threat, in your view?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, based on my personal observations as I passed through the town, I realised that there were very few Serb troops there. And my second observation was that there was a huge number of people there, captives, prisoners, who were all gathered in one place and that as for the Serbs, there were mostly unarmed civilians there, not troops. And my layman's assessment was that it could happen, given the circumstances, that the prisoners could take the town. And that's why I said so to Mr. Beara. I thought that he would be able to give a better assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you just tell us whether you made this conclusion or this assessment on the basis of the fact that there was a huge number of captured soldiers, enemies of the Serbian army, and that there was a very few -- that there were very few soldiers from your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like you to look at line 13. I will read it out. "After we returned to the gates of the command building, he asked me whether I had a list of Muslims suspected of war crimes against Serbs. I said that I had only a book entitled the "Chronicles of Our Cemeteries" by Miroslav [as interpreted] Ivanisevic which has a list of all those people and witness statements and that I myself took part in gathering materials for this book, gathering witness statements from Serbs after Serb villages were burnt down." Thank you. Did I quote you correctly, and is this something that you said?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on what he told you and since you said that you wrote this book and -- or, rather, that you took part in gathering materials, that there were people there that were identified as war criminals; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can tell us as a lawyer whether, as an administrative worker in your brigade, whether this was in fact the right job for you, whether your abilities were utilized to the maximum in that post?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a difficult question. Could you please be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether it was logical for you to be given this task, or instructions, as a lawyer since as a lawyer you were in fact misplaced to make this assessment in line with the request made by Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we are looking at paragraph 2. It begins with the word "The next day ..." or "Around noon the following day ..." Let us look at line 10 where you say: "When persons were identified, I asked them where they were from, their direction of movement, and whether they knew where Naser's commanders have gone." My question is this: Why did you ask them where Naser's commanders had gone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Because it would make it possible to identify the location of their movement and facilitate their arrest in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it mean that those commanders had not surrendered and had left the territory where all the others that you took statements from were still there, or remained?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I did not know their whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In line 12, you say that as you questioned those people you learned that they had not been -- they weren't compromised in any way, they were not responsible of anything?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does that mean that none of them were handed over to anyone for further processing or prosecution by judicial organs because there was no need following this identification that you carried out on the basis of the book and the witness statements that were gathered in the book?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at paragraph 3. This is the paragraph where -- which talks about how Rasid -- Resid Sinanovic was brought to your office. And your description how you spoke to Rasid [as interpreted], you and your colleagues - well, I don't want to quote. My question is whether you and the other brigade personnel and your colleagues in the brigade and in the town who spoke to Resid, whether any of you did anything to Resid that was not in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Before I give you an answer, I have to correct you. It's not "Rasid," it's "Resid." Nobody harmed Resid in any way. He was not mistreated in any way while he was in my office on that day. I didn't do anything to him, and I can give you just one other name. We didn't do anything to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. There's no need to list any names, but I just asked you whether you knew of any threats or any harm to his person or to his safety while he was under your control in the office, because it says here, I found Resid in the office. And thank you very much for correcting me that his name is Resid and not Rasid. Thank you. Could you please state for the record once again whether he was treated in any way that would not be in line with the standards for the treatment of a person who is questioned about war crimes in Srebrenica while he was under your control in the office and in the contact with other people who came into your office?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Quite the contrary. He was offered coffee, he was given lunch, he was given anything that he might require, such as cigarettes and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we please look at page 5, paragraph 1 of the witness statement in the Serbian language. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here you say - I will just read line 4: "I would like to note that there was -- there were no reliable documents showing that Resid was in any way involved in the massacre, and I myself was certain of that because I had worked with Resid before the war and we were on good terms and I knew that he was a mild and honest man." My question to you is: Given this knowledge that you had about Resid, did anyone insult Resid in your presence?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, in this line of this paragraph, we are reading line 15, where you say: "Since the above-mentioned officers claimed that they were Specials, there could be no arguing with them because they were arrogant fellows, Specials, and it was better not to get on their wrong side. We accepted that fact, said good-bye to Resid, and gave him a pack of Morava cigarettes to take with him because we had nothing else to give him except bread and a bottle of water." Now, my question is whether you as a lawyer consider that he was treated in line with all the required procedures based on the documents that you had in the brigade and in the book that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us look at paragraph 3 on this page, page 5, where you say, in line 1: "I no longer followed Colonel Beara's orders because no one was brought in that day or later, and it was absurd for me to check the identity papers of people that they accidently brought in. While in the school, that is, the reception centre, there were several hundred people whose identity papers no one checked." Thank you. Now, my question is whether you did not want to obey Beara's instructions, or is it that there was no need to do that, to continue doing what you had been doing in your office?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I followed Beara's instructions after Resid and five or six other people. Nobody else was brought in, so I didn't have anyone to work with. And it was rather absurd for me to wait for those two or three people to be brought in. And in the school I could have been given a security detail and then ordered to go there, to the reception centre, because there were many people there to check whether there were any responsible for anything. So it was really absurd for me to go on waiting there, given the heat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, were you the only lawyer in your brigade who dealt with moral, religious, and legal issues, as you stated in the first paragraph of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was not the only one. There was also Major Ratko Jevtic, but he was unexperienced because he was a recent graduate, he did not really have any practical experience, so that's why I did most of the work as the desk officer. And he was the assistant commander for the same sphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So, on the whole, in your brigade, did you do most of the work identifying possible war crimes suspects among the captives, or was there any other lawyer involved in that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were no other lawyers, but there was Momir Nikolic, the security officer. He did the same job, but as a security officer. But he is not a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You mentioned Momir Nikolic. And in paragraph 3, line 5 of your statement, that's at page 5, you say: Since after Momir Nikolic's incomplete statement in The Hague, a great material and moral damage was inflicted on me as a respectable and honest man by the Yellow Press such as "Dnevni Avaz." And this is the first opportunity I have to tell the truth before a competent organ. Did I quote you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My next question is this: Based on what I've just read, it's not quite clear whether harm was caused to you after the statement was given and withdrawn or when. Perhaps you want to comment on it. Perhaps we should give you an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know when Nikolic withdrew his statement, but immediately after he gave the statement - and it's just one sentence that he handed Resid Sinanovic to me as a lawyer, and his statement ended with that. From the context of his statement, the tabloids drew this erroneous conclusion that Resid Sinanovic, after he was handed over to me, disappeared and that I was to blame. I don't know what happened to him. Now I no longer am concerned about that to such an extent after all these trials, the Blagojevic and Beara cases. It is quite clear that this fact was taken out of the context of Momir Nikolic's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I think that it is now clear to all of us what your treatment of this gentleman, Resid Sinanovic, was. Now, let us move on to paragraph 4 of this statement of yours at page 5, which speaks about the UNPROFOR soldiers surrendering to the troops of your brigade. I'm reading first and the second lines: "On the same day, the 13th of July, 1995, in afternoon, I noticed several UNPROFOR members outside the military police building and I learned that they had surrendered. With them were four or five military policemen who were providing security for them. I learned from the military policemen that they were supposed to be put in the Vuk Karadzic elementary school. And I advised the military police to engage themselves as much as they could in ensuring the security of the members of the Dutch Battalion and to give them their full attention and assistance, especially if any of them needed medical help. And that there should be no mistakes there. The policemen took my advice and said that Captain Momir Nikolic had given them the same orders and that everything would be all right." Thank you. End of quote. Now, my question is this: Can you just briefly tell us if there were any problems with these members of UNPROFOR who had surrendered themselves to the brigade HQ and who were with you on the 13th, and whether you and the policemen and Nikolic treated them as you stated here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm still not sure whether they surrendered or just crossed over to our side, because they had weapons, they had rifles. And I would know if any of them had been mistreated. So after they were accommodated for a day or two, they were allowed to leave and depart for Holland. I know that they were escorted and that they were supposed to have a flight from Zagreb. As for their security or anything else, there were no incidents at all that would indicate anything like this. They were taken care of and provided with everything possible. They had good accommodation in the other school that was next to the health centre. It was called Vuk Karadzic, as there were some problems with the name earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As you said in your previous answer that they had weapons with themselves, does that mean that weapons were not taken away from them at the moment when you saw them? Did you see them carry the weapons, or did you see the weapons separately from them?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I could see that they had weapons, they had helmets, they had transport bags, equipment; they had everything on themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As you said that you are still unsure whether they had surrendered or were taken prisoners, as usually weapons are seised from prisoners, I'm asking you now, Who did you learn from that they had surrendered themselves? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Once again, it is difficult to answer. I did not learn that they had surrendered themselves. But from the membership commander, I heard that the interpreter told him, as both of us did not speak English, told him that they had crossed over to our side because of an incident in the villages around Srebrenica and that they had not surrendered themselves. It is logical that if they had the weapons with themselves, that they had not surrendered themselves but had crossed over to our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if you know or if you knew back then that there were members who fired on the 9th and the 10th and the 13th on the members of the VRS in the protected zone of Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: At the time when you saw them, did you personally know that the members of UNPROFOR in Srebrenica were requested to attack members of the VRS, and was that the reason for them to surrender themselves, because they did not want to attack?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not present in a situation where they would be requested either to attack or not to attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just briefly tell us, for the record, and so that we can finish this subject, whether, according to your knowledge then and now, the VRS treated these members of UNPROFOR who were taken prisoners or who had crossed over or who surrendered themselves, as we don't know?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm completely certain that they were treated properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please look at page 4, line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Which discusses how Beara told you that, as you had the book the "Chronicle of our Cemeteries" in which it contained the list of persons that committed crimes, that you should find out whether there were any such persons among the prisoners. If it is necessary, you can read it. And please tell us something more about this book, a "Chronicle of our Cemeteries" which you used in accordance with instructions provided by Beara. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: The "Chronicle of our Cemeteries," the author of which is Milovoje Ivanisevic from Belgrade, is a result of statements which were taken from villagers of Serb populated villagers that were attacked with all the consequences that followed. That means many soldiers and civilians killed, plundered, and torched villages, and such statements were given to a commission which investigated war crimes. That was a commission of Republika Srpska and also there was one in Yugoslavia. I don't know the exact title, but it was the commission that was set up by legitimate state organs. As for Milivoj Ivanisevic, I remember well that he was authorised by Ms. Biljana Plavsic, who was then the president, he had a permission that was stamped and signed that he would have access to documents and as an authorised person, he would visit and say what he was interested in. So that, as I know much about this work taking statements and assessing the validity and quality of statements, because I had a lot of experience with that due to my profession, at the request of both Milivoj Ivanisevic and the representative of the commission of Republika Srpska, I took statements from civilians and soldiers after attacks had been mounted against Serb populated villages. There was also a form that would be filled out with information about the place that had been attacked and the casualties, and that would be enclosed. They were provided with this, and so Milivoj Ivanisevic compiled this book, the "Chronicle of our Cemeteries," in which he laid out the chronology of attacks and casualties and historical reasons for all these incidents. I have read that book. I have that book. I had it on that day. But, like with any other book, the author exhausted everything that was possible. He included all the statements. And there were several statements that mentioned by Resid Sinanovic, but I believe them not to be valid at all. I can explain that if you'd like me. But that was not your question, so it is up to you to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As you and I know with we were talking about ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show 1D223 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we do that, Mr. Tolimir, you used the pages 1, 2, and 5 of the previous document which were not admitted into evidence yet because we only admitted pages 3 and 4. Are you tendering the pages 1, 2, and 5?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the moment, we are not sure if the whole document was admitted during examination-in-chief or only pages 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. As this was a witness statement, I just -- and it was only used in part by the Defence, I only offered those short parts, having Rule 92 bis and other rules in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You tendered only the pages 3 and 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. So far I have been speaking about the statement of this witness, and I would tender it in its entirety. But I wanted you to have a look, together with the witness, at the book in the compilation of which he participated. Thank you. I would tender the entirety of this statement into evidence, and then later on we will talk about specific pages of the book. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, could he state the grounds for which he is offering it, because if we are offering all the statements or many of the statements of all the witnesses that are coming here, that really undercuts the whole adversarial and civil law system that we are working under. If there's a particular reason that it may assist the Court, absolutely. But just -- it seems like they're just coming in for the sake of coming in. And you're going to be buried with this material if that continues. In addition, just reading material back to the witness and having him repeat it really doesn't get us anywhere. And it's actually not even evidence for your consideration. It just comes in that he said something to a police officer. It would be much shorter and simpler if he would just ask the witness the question that's in the report. He will get the answer and he will get it under oath to the Chamber, which is a more direct way than getting it through the police report. Police reports could be useful for him, and there are a number of ways that it could be, but the way he's doing it is not helpful for himself, the way he is doing it, because it's really not even evidence. It's just evidence that he said something to a police officer. And I'm sorry to take the Court's time on that, but it's going to be a long trial, and I just wanted the General to understand that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, on several occasions, I told you as well, it's not the best way just to read documents into the record which we have received already. But I would like to ask the Registrar if we have the whole document admitted or only pages 3 and 4 yet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, up to now, as on the request of the Prosecution, we have pages 3 and 4. You used, in addition, pages 1, 2, and 5. Is it not the best way to receive these three additional pages so that we have an entire impression of that, and not the whole document. I have no idea how many pages there are in the whole document, but I think you should decide that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There are only six pages in total, I'm told, and, therefore, the whole document will be received with the number already given, P646. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we now please look at 1D223 in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D223 is a book, the "Chronicle of Our Cemeteries," which was published in Bratunac in 1994. The author is Mr. Ivanisevic, and the publisher is the commission for collecting evidence against -- evidence of violations against humanitarian law. The witness collected some of the information for this book as he testified during cross-examination. Thank you. The text of this book is in e-court, and it can be reached via the website bibliotekaonline.com, which means libraryonline.com.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is there a translation of a part of that? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we currently do not have a translation of this document, but we have tried to learn if any sections of the book have been translated so that I hope we will inform the Trial Chamber about this as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could deal with this problem as follows: You just put questions to the authenticity of this book. And without using a part of the book, try to get what you want from this witness about the content. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would ask the witness to tell us whether he collected any information for this book and whether he is mentioned in the book as a witness who participated in this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I did collect a part of the materials for this book. I think that on one of the initial pages Mr. Milivoj Ivanisevic listed me as one of the associates who took part in collecting the materials for this book. It was not just me; he had a number of associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please have a look at page 7 to confirm the authenticity of the participation of this witness in collecting the materials for this book? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is one of the pages of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You can see in line 2 of the first page where it says, in the penultimate words: "Zlatan Celanovic, we wish to thank these persons for their personal engagement, among many other witnesses from the Bratunac municipality." Is it correct that all these people took part in collecting materials for this book?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Please let me just have a look first. Yes, I know them all. And I know that they were engaged in collecting the materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber in what way were you engaged when you collected materials for this book? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: By taking statements from witnesses who witnessed crimes committed against the Serbian people, civilians, and soldiers who were massacred or killed while defending their villages from witnesses who had survived and who were from the Serbian villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber whether at pages 124 to 128 of this book there are names -- or, rather, statements of victims. Could you please look at page 124-168, thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. What am I supposed to answer regarding this page of the book?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, if the pages that I just quoted to you, 124 through 168, whether they contained the witness statements?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can just see a part of a statement by Marko Slijvcevic [phoen], and I can't see anything else. Could we please just scroll down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move to the next page of this book in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This was page 124, which contained the first name that you read, and then there's 125, 126, and -- through to 168. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can see that these are texts that are termed as statements, but I do not have any authentic statements that would be signed. But this is how it's done in a book, how it's published.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, is it up to the author how to present it, how to present what you collected?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably, yes. It's enough for him to state the author of the statement and the original of the statement that was signed, he probably had in his files.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, based on what you know, what was the nature of the crimes against Serbs in the events described in this book in the area of Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Milici; and what kinds of scenes were described by various witness, in particular witnesses that you yourself interviewed? If you could give us a striking example, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I should start with the saddest example that will show us what kind of crimes were committed. A crime is a crime regardless of who the victim is. If somebody suffers in a conflict under the conventions under humanitarian law, those people should not suffer. And that goes primarily to women and children, even soldiers, if they surrendered. I remember a statement made by a woman from a village in the Srebrenica area; I can't recall the exact name of the village. One of the first victims was in fact her son; maybe it was the hamlet of Gnjilane in Srebrenica. He was first captured and then he was tortured. He was burnt with gas torches and he was then handed over to the demarcation line. He was brought there in a cart, in a wheelbarrow, in fact, in pieces. If they wanted to kill him, they could have just killed him. They didn't have to dismember him. Well, I don't know who actually did it. There was a war going on. But there were so many statements of that nature. For instance, the survivors from the Bjelovac village, from Zagone [phoen], from Kravica, from various villages in the Srebrenica area, many civilians, women, children, were killed, houses were burned down, looted. It was just a terrible, terrible image of war. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I would like us to move to page 56 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will quote just a part of it because I don't want to ask you in too great a detail. But let me just read a passage, six lines in total. It's paragraph 2, where it says: "Many of the persons who had been killed and who were exchanged or were in other ways recovered from the place where they were killed showed evidence of burns, charred body parts, their throats had been slit, their skulls had been shattered, their arms and legs had been fractured, their heads had been -- they had been decapitated. Often, victims were massacred, mutilated after they were already dead. Men were circumsised and castrated and women were raped before they were killed. Their butchered and burned bodies are testimony to ..." and so on. Now, my question based on what I just read to you is the following: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber whether those descriptions and conclusions are accurate and what they were based on in this book, whether there is any evidence to support those claims? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some conclusions are accurate because I myself know that those things happened, but I cannot really state that all the conclusions here are correct, because they were based on the statements made by people who were interviewed by other people, not by me. But, in fact, Dr. Veljko Macisic [phoen] could confirm or deny the accuracy of those statements because he worked in the healthcare centre and examined and did postmortems of the victims in some cases, and he was able to determine the kind of injuries and how they were inflicted and when. So I wouldn't really like to give you a blanket confirmation here. But I do know that there were some cases of that nature, where bodies were mutilated. I myself saw some of those cases in the healthcare centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we please look at page 67 in e-court. It's the part of the book entitled "The Ideological Leaders, Officials, Commanders, and Direct Perpetrators of the Crimes." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, we can see it here on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 66 to narrow this down. I don't want us to get too broad a scope. Just one passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, if I could ask the General under what purpose this material is being offered? What is his legal theory as to the relevance of this? Because there are certain prohibitions under certain kinds of relevance and others are not. So I think he should -- it's incumbent upon him to state his grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the Chamber would like to know, as well, what's the purpose of this book, this document in B/C/S, shown to the witness and the questions you have put to him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have dealt with this in our pre-trial brief, noting that the Defence and the Prosecution are at odds when it comes to some adjudicated facts that were put forward by the Prosecution and facts as they existed on the ground pertaining to the crimes committed by both sides. This is a book that the witness worked on, and he speaks about this in his statement. He identified people, he checked people, the prisoners, to check whether there were any identified perpetrators among them. And this is the only witness who can reliably tell us what he used as a basis for that. And he said that he didn't identify anyone. But this is all by way of proof that this was a professional doing a professional job, as a lawyer, of actually identifying those who committed crimes among those who took part in the fighting. And this is why we are trying to use this book through this witness who took part in gathering material for it to show that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That provided no answer to the question. Clearly this witness used this book, and information has been gathered in the book. My question was more related to the use of the horror and the gore and the individual crimes that he keeps mentioning which, of course, the Prosecution has never contested. Naser Oric was on trial here, that some terrible things were done by the Muslims. But why is he going over and over and over this gore? Is it a tu quoque situation? Is it the Muslims deserve to be butchered because they were so horrible? It is to prove that this was a revenge crime, not a genocide crime? I mean, why is -- what is his legal relevance for this material? We understand that the book was used by this person, that it's come in that way; that's no problem. But this repeated use of taking us through this horror, is my -- is why -- what is the relevance of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. What the Prosecutor has just told us and what he's asked, what was it all about? The Defence never used the tu quoque, eye-for-an-eye argument and never put -- pitted those crimes against the crimes of the other side. It's just trying to portray equitably everything that happened in around the Srebrenica zone and is using this witness, since according to his own statement he was involved as a lawyer on gathering information from direct participants of the events from witnesses. And he testified to that effect here. And we never said that we were trying to present an eye-for-an-eye or tu quoque arguments here. And this is what Mr. McCloskey is trying to put to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
