utterances.text: That's helpful in the degree now we know some reasons why he is not putting it forward. And that's, of course, appreciated. And we understand that it's important to get a feel for the area and what the sides are doing to each other. We are not -- we don't disagree; and, of course, we do agree. We helped prosecute Naser Oric. But I think we're at the point where enough is enough with this, unless he can show some particular relevance to it, especially since it's not a matter that's major contested. But he still hasn't given us a reason. Unless that's it, just to show the environment, which I understand, and is why I haven't objected until this point. Because I agree that he has every right to do that. But I think that the environment has been created fully and that any more getting into the -- it just becomes pure vilification of one side versus the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we are now at a time when the next break is -- has to be taken. I think you should think about the concerns of the Prosecution during the break. And taking into account the time you have used already for cross-examination, you indicated up to two hours, you should think about that, the best use of the time you have for cross-examination. We adjourn and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I'm sure you have used the time to consult your legal advisor. Please carry on with your cross-examination. And I see on the transcript we didn't resume at 2.00, but 1 and two minutes. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. A little while ago, the Prosecutor asked the Defence why this was relevant. If we need to say why it is, let me state it now. If it is not necessary, then I will continue with my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be helpful if you could give certain reasoning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. There are many reasons why what we are discussing with this witness is relevant. Some of the reasons are the following ones: Firstly and primarily, this could assist us all to understand, both the Trial Chamber and all the participants in this trial, why the protected zone of Srebrenica was established and why the Muslims from the surrounding areas escaped into this zone. Also, why later on they wanted to make a breakthrough at any cost, without waiting for anything else. That is one reason. It is also relevant in order to establish the context of the events that took place in 1995. The Defence and the Prosecution do not agree about many of these things. Firstly, the Prosecution has a thesis about ethnic cleansing carried out by the the Serbs in the territory of the eastern Podrinje. And they even said that the military activities of the VRS are based on that. You can see that in their motion that's in paragraph 10. Further on, war criminals, which we talked about when I tendered page 67, and the ideological leaders who are mentioned here and whom this witness tried to identify among the prisoners, are listed in this book. They were the military authorities in Srebrenica in the period when it was a demilitarised zone. They co-operated with UNPROFOR as well, and many witnesses brought here by the OTP are familiar with the incidents in this period. Thirdly, this could also assist us to understand the behaviour of the Muslim authorities in Srebrenica in the relevant time-period, I mean both the civilian and military authorities, and when they made the decisions that we talked about, and when they held meetings at the post office building, which was discussed with a witness yesterday. I would ask you to consider the relevance of this document from all aspects. I now asked for page 67 to be shown on the screen and to be tendered. It talks about ideological leaders, commanding officers, and it is from this book. It was a basic document from which this witness, in a specific given situation that he testifies about, questioned the prisoners of war. There are many other relevant things, but if you allow me, I would continue with additional two or three questions, and with that I would finish the cross-examination of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir, with your questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we please show page 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see it now. I began reading it. And it says: "During the armed conflicts which took place in this territory, the presence of Muslim military units or armed formations which came from or originated from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina was never noted. On the contrary, all testimonies, both from the Serbian and from the Muslim side," and please turn to the next page, "show that in the area of Bratunac, Milici, Skelani, and Srebrenica municipalities, only the armed forces established with local Muslim population were active." On the basis of what I just read out, my question for the witness to be the following: Does this correspond with the situation in Srebrenica and the surrounding villages? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please wait a moment. There is a problem with the microphone. Now you should continue. We didn't hear anything yet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not agree with the formulation set out in the book, namely Srebrenica was the zone and the place into which refugees from Zvornik and partly from Visegrad and some other municipalities did come. And the armed forces which attacked out of Srebrenica were not only composed of the population coming from the town and the municipality of Srebrenica, but also refugees from other municipalities who were accommodated in Srebrenica. Therefore, it was not just local population that set up the armed forces; there were other people as well. That was the information that I had, and that is my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please show page 69 in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In your statement, you said - and we have just discussed that - that to Beara's question whether you had any list of persons, Muslims who were suspected of war crimes, you responded by saying that you have the book, which we can now see in e-court, and that the list of such persons is laid out systematically in the book. And it begins on page 69 in the electronic edition of this book. It continues, but we can see the first page here. My question is this: When you told Beara that you could use Ivanisevic book, did you have in mind precisely the list that we can now see in e-court in front of us? And the list has a total of 53 pages. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was easier for me that way because I had some names in my mine that was a result of my work when taking statements. So I knew some names by heart. But it was easier for me to use the book, and that was it. I couldn't know it all. There were people about whom I could only learn from the book because other people had collected information about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I used the book as an easier way to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see the page that is in front of us, page 69. We can see in e-court the idealogical leaders, officials, and organisers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we have a look at page 76, please. So we can skip around seven pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here it says, at the bottom, the commanders; the names of persons who were in command positions are listed here. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move another ten pages onwards and have a look at page 85 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the title here which says "Direct Perpetrators." Does the list contain the persons who were direct perpetrators of crimes on the basis of which you conducted the checks?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please show page 105 in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here we can see that the title on this page is "Looters," and so and so forth. But we can see the specific names of persons who looted Serb villages. Thank you. I wouldn't go on leafing through the list, but was this book the basis for the task which Colonel Beara issued to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a basis for me, because it was the result of a collection of materials about the incidents that we are talking about. A number of people were engaged in this, and I couldn't know of all these people. I only knew those that I learned about in my personal work. So as a systematic overview, the book served as a basis for me to discharge my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender 1D223 into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, what is the position of the Prosecution to this motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I join the General in offering this book into evidence, and though I -- trying to get it translated will be very difficult, perhaps they can pick out particular appropriate passages they think reflect the most important information. I know the CLSS people will not want to be able to take on a book of this sort, so we will discuss the matter and try to reach a good arrangement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the moment, we have no translation of the book, even not portions of the book. This is one problem. Therefore we will only mark it for identification. On the other hand, we see that Mr. Tolimir is tendering the whole book as evidence; there's no objection by Mr. McCloskey, but he -- Mr. McCloskey said "I'm trying to get it --" no, sorry. "Perhaps they," the Defence, "can pick out particular appropriate passages they think reflect the most important information." We will not decide at the moment to save court time about if we receive the whole book or parts of the book. We invite the parties to make a common application which parts of the book should be tendered and which parts not, taking into account the burden for the translation unit of the Tribunal. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir. No, sorry. Ms. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D223 will be D74, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My legal advisor will comply with your instructions, and I don't think that the CLSS would have many problems because these are just the names of victims and villages and there's no need to translate it. 90 per cent of the book comprises those names and documents, it's just some conclusions that need to be translated. Thank you. I would like to thank this witness for his professionalism and propriety in the time-period, and also to the sincerity of his answers that he provided, regardless of whether they favour the Prosecution or the Defence. I would like to wish you a safe trip home, God bless you, thank you very much. I would like to thank the interpreters, the Trial Chamber, and I would also like to thank on behalf of the Defence to the Prosecution and everyone else that assisted us today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Could we put back P643 on the -- on e-court. That should be that aerial image.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, you had identified, with an X for us, the Vuk Karadzic School where you saw prisoners on the 13th; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've also said that the Dutch Battalion people that you saw in Bratunac were housed at a school, and I think you said it was the school next to the health centre, and I think you said that that was the Vuk Karadzic School. And I know that Vuk Karadzic is an important person and he gets named a lot of things and that has changed over the years a lot, so could you clarify -- can you find the school where the Dutch Battalion were staying for those days on the map so we can just be perfectly clear. First of all, were they staying at the same school prisoners were staying at?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No. There's mistake in the name of the school. The school where the prisoners were is the Branko Radicevic school. I made mistakes earlier, but now I'm sure; I'm certain about that. And the school where the DutchBat troops, UNPROFOR troops, were put up was the Vuk Karadzic School. I can find it here mand I can mark it here on the aerial photo. It just needs to be zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If we could zoom in. I think just showing us where this school is is probably the best at this point. Better stop there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please scroll down a little bit and to the right. In fact, yeah, the opposite. Just a moment. Yes, I can actually identify the location. Should I mark it? Should I circle it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, make just a big circle.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And just again, so it's clear to all of us, put a big X at that school that you saw prisoners.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, no, I made a mistake. I wanted to mark that school with an X. And now as for the school where I saw the prisoners, I have to stand up. It's a little bit awkward because I'm left-handed. This is the school. Okay. Now, I circled the school where I saw the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we've got -- why don't you put a letter A next to the school where you saw the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you remember what the name of the school under the letter A was called back in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Branko Radicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You sure it wasn't called the Vuk Karadzic school back then?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I will give you a broader explanation in my answer, because I don't want to make a mistake here. May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: This building that I've just circled was a school that used to be called Vuk Karadzic. And it was the only elementary school in Bratunac. However, later on, because the population increased, the other building was made, another school building - I made a circle to mark that, the big circle - and then the new school came to be called Vuk Karadzic, and the old school building was now -- the school there, was now named Branko Radicevic. That's what I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: And perhaps you can identify the buildings on the basis of their size and the markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that helps us.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: So in the smaller building - I will now put a dot next to it - this is where the prisoners were. And the other building that I marked with an X, this is where the DutchBat troops were located, most of them. Two or three of the soldiers were put up in the dorm of the military police platoon. They spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you just for a better understanding. You told us that the other building was made, another school building. When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the war. I can't really remember the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, were you aware that some of these Dutch soldiers were housed at the Hotel Fontana that you've already shown us on the map?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you aware of where the main contingent of the Dutch soldiers were housed in the Srebrenica/Bratunac area? I mean generally. Where was their base normally, where they all lived?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Their base was in Potocari. And I think that the main contingent was there. But they had smaller centres in other villages where -- from which they patrolled and did other things, but their main base was in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know why these soldiers housed at the school in Bratunac were not allowed to go back to their main base in Potocari after they were captured or turned themselves in or over?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know why they were not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear, while you were there near the Bratunac headquarters during these days, that the VRS threatened to kill Dutch soldiers held in VRS custody if air-strikes continued? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never heard any threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear that threats were made, was that talk among the soldiers, was it reported to you by your boss, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not hear about any threats from anyone on any occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. The book, "The Chronicle of Our Graves," were the facts and incidents and similar things noted in that book, were those sorts of things well known to the population of Bratunac at the time in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot agree that they were well known to the population because those were the facts known only to those who gathered the statements and the inhabitants of the villagers who were actually victims. Well, it's impossible for the rest of the population, the general population, to know everything. They knew in general what was going on, but they didn't know the names of the victims and perpetrators, because if you say something, a fact of general knowledge, then it should be known to everyone or almost everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not asking if the population knows everything. Not -- no one knows everything. But you would agree with me that the population was generally aware of the allegations of horrible war crimes by the Muslims of Srebrenica during the war; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In fact, many, many of the population of the Serbs that lived there had lost sons and fathers during the fighting that had occurred from 1992 all the way up to 1995; that's true too, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that it was very natural for that population to be very angry and very upset about what they perceived as horrible crimes perpetrated against their family members and neighbours and friends?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's only natural for them to be angry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, in fact, wasn't it part of the moral, legal, and religious affairs to propagate information about these atrocities so that soldiers were aware of it when they went to fight?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the publication by General Gvero called "A Silk Knot for Alija" that he sent out to the VRS? General Gvero, as you know -- well, sorry, just -- if you could answer that question.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never have held this document in my hands, and this is indeed the first that I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since this was not dealt with in the Prosecutor's examination-in-chief, if he wants to ask questions, then he should show this book to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to ask Mr. McCloskey if he wants to -- if he tenders this marked aerial photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President, for reminding me of that. We do need to put that in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received before we lose these markings.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P654.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber didn't see exactly to which part of the cross-examination you were referring by putting the last question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the -- General Tolimir spent a good amount of time -- it's best that I explain this outside the presence of the witness, I think, just for the fairness of everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we break for that purpose, how much time do you need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Five minutes -- I shouldn't -- should do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, we should ask the witness to leave the courtroom for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's two issues. One, General Tolimir argued at length on what this book was all about and why it was relevant to his case, and what I'm getting to goes directly to contradict that. But more in particular, he spent a fair amount of time suggesting and showing that this witness never did anything to harm Resid Sinanovic. And what I'm pointing out now is that there was a very well known environment of hate between these sides. And as he has already said, there were very few people guarding the Muslim prisoners. And that in that environment of hate this witness would have been in the situation to know he was turning over Resid Sinanovic and these men to a situation that was very dangerous for them because of that environment of hate. And that's what I wanted to ask him about. Was he not aware that these men were in danger. He talked a lot about how dangerous the Muslims were on Bratunac, but I want to bring out how dangerous Bratunac was on the Muslims. You will see evidence in this case of the over 100 bodies that came out of the Vuk Karadzic School from Serb civil protection witnesses that pulled those bodies. So that's pretty much it. But these are the big issues of the case. They touched on them. I want to get back at them a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what that has to do with the publication of General Gvero called "A Silk Knot for Alija"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my position that this book that he's talked about is a foundational element in the Serbs vilification of the Muslims which is, as you'll hear from this case, is a critical part of the war effort, both in my view to instill soldiers' willingness to fight and in also instilling the effort to have them commit crimes. Before you can commit any kind of mass slaughter like this, it's historical that the perpetrators will vilify their victims. This book is part of that vilification process. That's why I offer it into evidence. It's clear as a bell. This man is an officer in moral, legal, and religious affairs. General Gvero is the general in charge of moral, legal affairs. He is a colleague of General Tolimir. He wrote one of the most insidious propaganda vilification pieces of the war called "A Silk Knot For Alija" on the very similar nature of this book that the General wants in. And as an officer and a lawyer, there's a very good chance he would have read this. And in which case I would have provided it to you so you could see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This -- I think this is quite sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry for arguing so much, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just wanted to have the link to this book which was mentioned in your last question to which Mr. Tolimir was objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you don't deal with this book any longer, this specific book, the witness has said he has no knowledge about that at all, never seen it. And it's the first time I hear of it. We should try to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Because of his answer, I had no intention to bring it for -- if he'd seen it, I would have asked him about it and dug it up for you; but he didn't, so it's not relevant. Then we could leave this problem. And the witness should be brought in again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, were you aware that Muslim men and women were bused towards Kladanj on these days, the 12th and 13th of July specifically?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure about the 12th. I saw them pass by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you see the -- many of the civilians of Bratunac, including women and other people, throwing stones at the Muslim buses and saying bad things to them as the buses went by?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No. This did not happen at the place where I was, the place where I was and from which I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear reports of this happening? This would have clearly been a military police matter, I'm sure you'll agree with me.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that there were some events of that nature or attempts to do that, for instance, in Potocari when people were put on to the vehicles, but that on the 12th, the UNPROFOR members prevented that as did the military police and the police that were deployed there from the Bratunac Brigade and from other units. That's all I know about that from my conversations with the military policemen in the subsequent period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you were aware, then, of the environment of hate present in Bratunac when you turned over Resid Sinanovic and the other Muslims to go be put in that school?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: With that environment of hate and the very few people guarding it as you've described, weren't those Muslims also in danger?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say that. They were put in facilities, secured and guarded by the Republika Srpska army troops, and if any attacks came from the outside or if there were any problems from the inside, they were there to deal with it. But there were no assaults by the citizens on the facilities where the prisoners were housed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wanted to say that this witness did not hand over Resid and that again this will harm him in the environment where he lives. He had just been brought to this witness's office by the relevant organs and was then taken away by the Special Police. This witness has nothing to do with any surrender of anyone into anyone's hands, because the witness himself explained to us that he has had problems because of some statements that were made that were not entirely accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But this is not really an objection to the question the Prosecutor has put to the witness, which is answered. We should come to an end, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, did you -- were you aware of the evidence -- you said you saw -- you were familiar with the Blagojevic trial, the Popovic trial. Were you aware of the evidence from Bratunac civil protection people of picking up over 50 bodies from in and around the school that you have marked where the prisoners were held?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of any evidence except that at one of the trials I was asked the question whether I knew about this incident, that on the 12th or the 13th more than 50 people were executed at this school, but I didn't know that. And I repeat once again that I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Last question: The evidence in this case which is now before the Trial Chamber shows that five of the six people who you interviewed that day, including Resid Sinanovic, showed up in mass graves in the Zvornik area. Do you know anything about how those men that you interviewed ended up in mass graves?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how they ended up in mass graves. If they were found in the vicinity of Zvornik, it means that they were probably transported from the Branko Radicevic school in the direction of Zvornik, but after the police had taken them and handed them over at the collection centre or reception centre - I'm not sure how best to formulate that. But how they came to end up in Zvornik or the surrounding area of Zvornik is something I don't know. I have no information about that; I can only assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question for the witness. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Witness, I go through the summary that the OTP has given to us regarding your previous statements and I can see that you are a trained lawyer and that in July 1995 you were a member of the Bratunac Brigade and you were a desk officer at the department for legal and moral affairs. I have a point of clarification to put to you. I would like to know whether you read law in a university or in a school of higher education?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the faculty of law of the Belgrade university.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Very well. And what I would like to know is whether you were a member of armed forces in July 1995, and if so, of which army and at which rank?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the armed forces of the Army of Republika Srpska. In order to make it clearer, I will use the western term: I was a private; that was my status. So I was a soldier with no rank. And if I may just add something to make it even clearer. May I? Thank you. The Prosecutor mentioned the word officer, but an officer can be interpreted both as an official and as an officer. I was a desk officer in the sense that I was an official who was in charge of religious and legal affairs, so it is just an error in terminology. I was a desk officer, but you do not have to be a military officer in order to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: So just to clarify, you were within the brigade, but you were not wearing any uniform and you did not have any rank; is that correct? Apparently your answer was yes. Very well. So I would like to know whether you are retired now or whether you still work within the army?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I did wear a uniform as a soldier throughout the time I spent there. I held no rank, and I'm not retired. I'm still young.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: But you left the army, didn't you? You work as a civilian these days, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I've been demobilised, so the answer is yes. Yes. If I may add something to make it clearer: I was a civilian at the outbreak of the war, but as I had served the army in the former Yugoslavia, that is to say, the Yugoslav People's Army, I was made a reserve soldier. As a middle-aged man, I was mobilised during the time of the armed conflict. After that, I was demobilised and, therefore, I became a civilian again and I was doing a civilian job. So I'm not someone who was employed in the army and who would be retired as military personnel. It was my misfortune that I was a lawyer, so I had to do all kinds of work, because they needed someone who had a BA in law and they needed someone like that to do that kind of work. And I also had experience from the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. You answered all my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You will be pleased to hear that this concludes your examination. Thank you that you were able to come to The Hague again and to provide us with your answers and your knowledge. Thank you again. Two very short matters. And I apologise for the other Trial Chamber who is sitting in this courtroom this afternoon. We have received, with the previous witness, two versions of the former transcript. This is P629, under seal, and P630. I think the letter, P630, should be marked but not admitted because it's the same content and it was in closed session; it shouldn't be in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. And before you go, we had to cancel Witness 103, which we've informed the Defence. And so we have one more witness tomorrow, a Bosnian witness, and then we -- who's number 110, and then Mr. Blaszczyk will continue his -- I believe he is in cross-examination now for the Drina Corps collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber would appreciate if you could mail to the Defence and to the Chamber what you are doing with -- which witnesses you are calling for the rest of this week and the beginning of next week so that we have an overview. And please indicate what to do with the exhibits provisionally tendered with Witness 103, which is PW-036.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have to adjourn very late today. And we will resume tomorrow morning, I think, in Courtroom I. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 8th day of July, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
